title: Rainy Day Cannabis: What to Enjoy When You're Stuck In
h1: Rainy Day Cannabis Ideas for a Cozy Day Indoors

body:
Rainy day cannabis is about slowing down: a gray afternoon, nowhere to be and time for an unhurried ritual at home. Maybe it's a soggy spring weekend or a lake-effect day in Michigan. Here's how to match a format to your indoor plans, whether that's flower, an edible, a vape or a topical after a warm bath, plus how to stock up without getting soaked. It's all for adults 21 and older.

## Why gray days and at-home cannabis rituals pair well

Rain clears the calendar. With no drive to make and no plans to keep, you can pick a format, take your time and pay attention to how it feels. Home is the right place for it anyway: Michigan law rules out using cannabis in public or while driving, so a day indoors suits the weather and the law alike.

## Rainy day cannabis flower for an unhurried afternoon

Flower suits a slow day because you can pace it, a little at a time with breaks in between. Shoppers often describe earthy, musky profiles as mellow and bright citrus or piney ones as lively. Those are impressions rather than tested effects, and strain names don't reliably predict how you'll feel, so go by aroma, the THC on the label and your own notes. Pick something you already know you enjoy, and keep the session easygoing.

## Edibles for a long indoor stretch

An edible suits a day with no plans because it unfolds slowly. Canada's chief medical officers of health warn that noticing an edible can take as long as 2 hours, and feeling all of it up to 4. So hold off on a second serving until the first one has clearly arrived. Michigan sets 10 mg of THC as the most an adult-use edible serving can hold, and if you're new, one serving or less is a sensible start. Our [edibles guide](/blog/what-are-marijuana-edibles/) covers the basics.

## Vapes for low-smell, low-effort sessions

A vape pen is the low-fuss option: no grinding, no ash and less lingering odor than smoke, which helps when the windows are shut. You'll feel a vape within minutes, so pause after a short draw before taking another. New to vapes? Our [vape pen guide](/blog/what-is-a-vape-pen/) explains the parts and setup.

## Concentrates: only for experienced consumers

Concentrates pack far more THC than flower, which makes them a poor choice for casual experimenting on a rainy day. If you already know how they affect you, keep amounts small and pace yourself. If you don't, stick with flower, a vape or a low-dose edible.

## Topicals and a warm bath: non-intoxicating options

Lotions, balms and other cannabis topicals go on the skin, and they aren't made to cause a high. In a small University of Bonn study, three volunteers rubbed two THC salves onto their skin every few hours for three days, and THC never showed up in their blood or urine tests. Transdermal patches are the outlier, because a patch is made to move cannabinoids through the skin into your blood, so check the label. A warm bath followed by a favorite lotion makes an easy ritual for a gray day. Our [topicals guide](/blog/guide-to-cannabis-topicals/) covers the different types.

## Indoor plans: movies, cooking, games and music

- **A movie marathon.** Line up a series or a stack of films; our [movie pairing guide](/blog/what-to-watch-for-marijuana-lovers/) has ideas.
- **Cooking.** A slow-simmered soup or a loaf of bread fills an afternoon. If you cook with cannabis, label anything infused and keep it well away from kids and pets.
- **Games.** A jigsaw puzzle, a board game or a long video game session.
- **Music.** A full album on good headphones, start to finish.

Keep snacks and water within reach, and keep your cannabis sealed in its original packaging.

## Shopping in the rain: order online for curbside pickup

Skip the wet walk across the parking lot. With High Society, you can shop your store's menu online, choose when to collect and check out from the couch. Pick curbside at checkout; a text will let you know when the order is waiting, so you can stay in the car until then. Keep your ID handy, since staff check it at every pickup. Start on [our shop page](/shop/), or find directions and hours on our [store locations](/dispensary-locations/) pages.

Head home before you open anything, and never drive after using cannabis, rain or shine. 21+ only. Please consume responsibly.

faq.q: What kind of strain suits a slow, rainy day?
faq.a: One you already know and enjoy. Shoppers often describe earthy, musky profiles as mellow and bright citrus or piney ones as lively, but those are impressions, not tested effects, and strain names don't reliably predict how you'll feel. Choose a THC level you're comfortable with and pace yourself.

faq.q: How long should I wait after an edible?
faq.a: Longer than you might think. It can take up to 2 hours before an edible registers and up to 4 before you feel its full effect, so don't add more until the first serving has arrived. Start with one serving or less; Michigan's adult-use servings hold 10 mg of THC at most.

faq.q: Will a cannabis topical get me high?
faq.a: No, not a lotion or balm. In one small study, volunteers who applied THC salves several times a day for three days had no detectable THC in blood or urine. Transdermal patches are another matter, since they're made to reach the bloodstream, so read the label before using one.

faq.q: Can I order ahead and pick up curbside?
faq.a: Yes. Place your order on your High Society store's online menu, choose when you'll come by and request curbside as you check out. A text lets you know when your order is ready. Bring a valid photo ID, because staff check it before every sale, including curbside handoffs.

review.notes: No pain-relief or mood claims for topicals or strains; strain descriptors are labeled as impressions. No public consumption suggested; driving line is safety plus law. Fact-check 2026-10-24: Independent check: the Canadian chief medical officers' statement re-opened by WebFetch; Hess 2017 abstract via E-utilities; Filipiuc 2023 full text via Europe PMC; vaping-odor user surveys (Malouff 2014, Etter 2015) via E-utilities; Michigan law against law-facts (public use, vehicles, edible limits, ID before every sale; cited michigan.gov and benchbook sources are the ones law-facts lists); High Society pickup against hs-facts.
